h1:
Getting to Koh Kood
How to arrive and get around the island
intro: Koh Kood sits at the far southern tip of Trat province, Thailand's second-largest island after Phuket and Koh Chang — but there's no bridge, so everyone arrives by boat. Almost every trip starts at Laem Sok pier in Mueang Trat district, about 320–340 km from Bangkok. Most people take a van or coach down to Trat first, then catch a ferry or speedboat for another 45 minutes to about an hour and a half. The big thing to know before you plan: Koh Kood is a long haul, and there's a monsoon season from roughly mid-May to mid-October when boats cut their runs and many places close. On the island itself the main road is a single concrete strip running the length of it, narrow and hilly in places. We've pulled together how to get there, real ballpark prices, and the distances between beaches so you can time everything before you set off.

blocks.html: First, understand that getting to Koh Kood always has two legs. The first leg is reaching Trat province on the mainland; the second is taking a boat across from Laem Sok pier over to the island. There's no airport on Koh Kood itself — the nearest is Trat Airport (Bangkok Airways), out near Khao Saming district, and even from there you still need ground transport to the pier. Once you've got these two legs straight in your head, timing and budgeting get a lot easier.

The most popular route is a van or coach from Bangkok down to Trat. Plenty of operators sell it as an all-in package — van + boat + songthaew right to your accommodation on the island, all on a single ticket — which is handy if you'd rather not change vehicles yourself several times. If you're driving your own car, you can leave it at the parking lot at Laem Sok pier and cross over without it.

items: Van / coach Bangkok–Trat — mainly departs from Ekkamai and Mo Chit stations, taking around 5–6 hours, with fares around ฿250–300 each way.

All-in package, van + boat + songthaew to your hotel — several boat companies, such as Boonsiri and Koh Kood Express, sell door-to-door tickets for around ฿1,100 per person each way. Booking ahead is more reliable.

Fly into Trat Airport — Bangkok Airways flies from Suvarnabhumi, with fares that swing with the season; once you land it's another 40–50 minutes by road to the pier. Good if you're short on time and have a bit more budget.
Drive yourself — Bangkok to Trat is about 320–340 km via the motorway / Bangna–Trat road, then turn off toward Laem Sok pier. There's an overnight parking lot charging around ฿50 a day.

blocks.title: Watch out — don't mix up the piers
blocks.html: Trat has several piers. The one for Koh Chang is Laem Ngop / Ao Thammachat, while almost all Koh Kood boats leave from Laem Sok pier — a different side entirely, about 30 km from Trat town. When you arrange a ride or call a taxi, say the pier name clearly so you don't end up at the wrong one and miss your boat.

blocks.text: Leg 2 — the boat across from Laem Sok to Koh Kood

blocks.html: From Laem Sok pier there are several main boat companies to choose from — both big catamaran ferries and speedboats. Most boats dock at Ao Salad pier on the north of the island, and some runs stop at Koh Mak on the way. Price and travel time vary by boat type.

items.name: Ferry / catamaran (Boonsiri · Koh Kood Express · Seadamco)
items.blurb: The big boats most people take — comfortable seating, shaded from sun and wind, and some have WiFi. Seadamco is a newer catamaran that does the crossing in about 45 minutes, while the others run roughly one to one and a half hours. In high season there are several runs a day, from late morning to late afternoon.
items.meta: About 45 min–1.5 hr · docks at Ao Salad

items.name: Koh Kood Princess
items.blurb: The cheapest ferry of the bunch — a little slower, but worth it if you're not in a rush. Good for backpackers or anyone watching the budget. It runs fewer departures than the others, so check the schedule well ahead.

items.name: Private speedboat / charter run
items.blurb: The fastest option, around 45 minutes to an hour, and good for big groups or anyone who wants exact timing. The per-head price runs higher than the ferry; chartering a whole boat round-trip for a group lands in the tens of thousands of baht, which works out when you split it several ways. When the swell is up, small boats slam around a lot — if you get seasick easily, take a big ferry instead.
items.price: From ฿1,200/person · charter in the tens of thousands

blocks.title: Boat fares usually include transfers
blocks.html: In high season many boat tickets bundle in a pickup from Trat town or your accommodation to the pier, plus a songthaew from the Koh Kood pier to your resort, all in the price. Before you buy, ask clearly whether the transfer to your accommodation is included, so you don't end up paying extra for a songthaew on the island.

blocks.text: Monsoon season — what to know before you book

blocks.html: I'll be straight with you: Koh Kood isn't beautiful year-round. The real high season is roughly October to mid-May — clear water, calm seas, every boat running. From mid-May to mid-October it's monsoon: frequent rain, big swells, boats running far fewer trips (some days none at all), and many resorts, restaurants and bike-rental shops closed for the whole season. If you're planning this stretch, phone the resort and the boat company to check every time — don't rely on the timetable on the website alone.

items: High season (Oct–mid-May) — all boats running, clear water, but busy and accommodation fills fast, so book ahead.
Monsoon (mid-May–mid-Oct) — fewer boat runs or none some days, many places closed, cheaper prices but you're gambling on the rain. Always check the status with the boat operator first.

Snorkelling and diving — tours out to Koh Wai and Koh Rang depend on the weather, and a big swell can get a tour cancelled. Don't put a snorkel tour on your last day, because if it's pushed back there's no backup day.

blocks.text: Getting around the island — motorbike, songthaew, resort transport

blocks.html: On Koh Kood the main road is a single concrete strip running about 9-plus km from Ban Klong Chao to Ban Ao Yai, passing the sights one after another — Klong Chao Waterfall, Klong Chao Beach, the giant tree, Ao Phrao and the viewpoints. But the turnoffs to some resorts and beaches branch into small lanes — some still dirt, some on steep climbs. How you get around depends on your style and how confident you are behind the handlebars.

items.name: Rent a motorbike
items.blurb: The most freedom — go wherever you like. Rentals run about ฿250–500 a day depending on the model and the shop, with petrol around ฿40–50 a litre from the small pumps on the island. Great if you ride confidently, but the road is narrow, hilly and slippery in spots when it rains. Wear a helmet and take it slow.

items.name: Songthaew / island taxi
items.blurb: Good if you don't ride a motorbike — flag one to a beach or waterfall trip by trip, or hire it for the whole day. The fare per trip runs around ฿500–2,500 depending on distance and number of stops. Agree on the price before you get in, every time.

items.name: Resort shuttle
items.blurb: Many resorts run a shuttle from the pier and to nearby sights — free at some places, a charge at others. Ask when you book your room what's on offer, so you don't have to arrange a ride for every single trip.

blocks.title: Take care riding a motorbike on the island
blocks.html: Koh Kood's road is wide enough for two songthaews to pass, true, but plenty of stretches are narrow, winding, and run up and down steep hills. Some beach access roads are gravel or very narrow concrete. If you're a beginner who doesn't ride confidently, avoid the steep sections or take a songthaew instead. At night the street lighting is limited and the phone signal is weak in spots, so head back before dark and check your route ahead of time.

Koh Kood looks small on the map, but driving around the main sights actually takes a fair while because the road winds and you have to go slow in places. The accommodation and restaurants cluster on the west side around Klong Chao Beach and Ao Tapao, while the giant tree and the waterfall sit further inland in the middle of the island. These rough distances help you plan each day.

items: Klong Chao Beach ↔ Ao Tapao — both on the west side, close together, about a 10–15 minute ride. This is the densest zone for accommodation, restaurants and beach bars.
Klong Chao Beach ↔ Klong Chao Waterfall — turn inland, about a 10 minute ride, then a short walk to the falls themselves.
Klong Chao Beach ↔ the giant tree (Makha tree) — deep in the forest in the middle of the island, about a 15–20 minute ride, with the final stretch on a narrow road.
Klong Chao Beach ↔ Ao Phrao / Ao Yai — head south along the main road, about a 20–30 minute ride, passing viewpoints and a fishing village.

Ao Salad pier ↔ the Klong Chao Beach zone — from the northern pier down to the main accommodation area, about a 20–30 minute ride. Normally the resort songthaew, or the one included in your boat ticket, drops you off.

blocks.text: Sample itinerary — getting the timing right

items.activity: Leave Bangkok by van/coach down to Trat
items.note: If you booked an all-in package, the van takes you straight to Laem Sok pier

items.activity: Reach Trat, transfer to Laem Sok pier
items.note: Allow at least 30–45 minutes to check in for the boat before departure

items.activity: Board the ferry/speedboat and cross over to Ao Salad pier
items.note: A big boat handles seasickness better when the swell is up

items.activity: Songthaew drops you at the resort, check in, rest up
items.note: Keep the first day easy — just the beach in front of your accommodation

blocks.label: Full day out
blocks.title: Rent a ride and loop the main sights

items.activity: Pick up your motorbike rental / book a songthaew for the day
items.note: Fill up with enough petrol — there are only a few pumps on the island

items.activity: Klong Chao Waterfall, then stop at the giant tree mid-island
items.note: The last stretch is narrow — ride slowly

items.activity: Head back for lunch in the Klong Chao Beach–Ao Tapao zone
items.note: The restaurants cluster on this side

items.note: Ride back before dark — street lighting is limited

faq.q: Which pier do you catch the boat to Koh Kood from?
faq.a: Almost all Koh Kood boats leave from Laem Sok pier in Mueang Trat district, about 30 km from Trat town. Be careful not to confuse it with Laem Ngop pier, which is the one for Koh Chang — they're on different sides.

faq.q: How much is the boat to Koh Kood, and how long does it take?
faq.a: The ferry/catamaran is around 600 THB each way and takes roughly 45 minutes to an hour and a half depending on the boat. The budget option, Koh Kood Princess, is around 400–500 THB. Speedboats start around 1,200 THB per person and are the fastest, at about 45 minutes to an hour.

faq.q: When should you avoid Koh Kood?
faq.a: During monsoon, roughly mid-May to mid-October — frequent rain, big swells, boats running fewer trips or none on some days, and many places closed for the season. If you're going then, always phone the resort and the boat company to check first. The high season with the clearest water is October to mid-May.

faq.q: Can you rent a motorbike on Koh Kood, and how much is it?
faq.a: Yes, around 250–500 THB a day depending on the model and the shop, with petrol about 40–50 THB a litre. The main road is easy to ride, but some stretches are narrow and steep, so beginners should ride slowly and wear a helmet. If you're not confident, take an island songthaew instead.

faq.q: If you don't ride a motorbike, how do you get around the island?
faq.a: Use an island songthaew/taxi — flag one trip by trip or hire it for the whole day, with fares around 500–2,500 THB depending on distance and number of stops. Always agree on the price before you get in. Many resorts also run a shuttle from the pier and to nearby sights.
